sections.h2: Where is Montgomery County and what does its housing market look like?
sections.html:
Montgomery County sits in south-central Illinois, with Hillsboro as the county seat and Litchfield as the largest city. It was formed in 1821 from parts of Bond and Madison counties and named for Richard Montgomery, a Revolutionary War general. The county covers about 704 square miles of land and borders Sangamon, Christian, Shelby, Fayette, Bond, Madison and Macoupin counties.

The population has drifted down from 30,104 in 2010 to 28,288 in 2020, and the Census Bureau estimates 28,076 for mid-2025. The median home value is modest, yet a seller still has to clear every open tax installment before closing.

Hillsboro's January lows average near 21 degrees and its July highs near 91, with a recorded range from minus 22 to 114. Freeze and thaw wear on roofs and foundations, so older houses in the county often show repair items an inspector will flag.

sections.h2: Which Montgomery County offices deal with property tax?
sections.html:
Four offices share the work, and each one answers a different question. The county's own pages split them this way:

  • Treasurer and ex-officio collector: bills, collects and distributes real estate, drainage and mobile home tax, and holds the annual tax sale. The office is on the first floor of the Historic Courthouse, Room 101, 1 Courthouse Square in Hillsboro, phone (217) 532-9521.
  • County Clerk and Recorder: computes the rate for each parcel, runs redemption of sold taxes and records deeds. Tax rate and redemption questions go to (217) 532-9530, and recording to (217) 532-9535.
  • Supervisor of Assessments: administers the assessment cycle, processes exemptions, assigns parcel numbers and assists with the senior forms. It sits in Room 201 and answers at (217) 532-9595.
  • Board of Review: hears assessment complaints and meets in the Supervisor's office.

The county's FAQ sends valuation questions to your township assessor, exemption and appeal questions to the Supervisor, rate questions to the Clerk and bill questions to the Treasurer. Calling the right desk first saves a transfer.

sections.h2: How do you pay a Montgomery County tax bill?
sections.html:
You can pay the Treasurer by mail, in person, by drop box, by phone or online. The Treasurer's page lists these routes:

  • Mail to Montgomery County Treasurer, 1 Courthouse Square, Room 101, Hillsboro, IL 62049.
  • In person at Room 101 of the Historic Courthouse.
  • The gray metal drop box on the north side of the courthouse, beside the fire escape.
  • The automated phone line at (217) 627-6183.
  • The online payment link on the Treasurer's page.

Montgomery County has also chosen, under Public Act 104-0553, to buy all delinquent real estate taxes itself as trustee for the taxing districts, starting with the 2025 taxes payable in 2026. Delinquent mobile home taxes still go to private buyers at the sale. Landowners who like to pay early can ask about the county's prepayment contract: a deposit is held in trust toward the coming bill, any shortfall is due by the second due date, and any excess is refunded, with the interest staying with the county.

sections.h2: When are Montgomery County property taxes due?
sections.html:
The due dates are printed on each year's bill, so read the stubs rather than a calendar from memory. State law treats the first installment as delinquent after the later of June 1 or the day after the date on the bill, and the second after the later of September 1 or the day after its printed date (35 ILCS 200/21-15). In a county of this size the interest is 1 1/2% per month or part of a month.

A payment postmarked on or before the due date is on time. The county's FAQ adds that taxes remain due whether or not a bill arrives, so a new owner who never received one still has to ask the Treasurer for the amount. To make sure the bill goes to the right person, ask the Treasurer to confirm who is listed as taxpayer of record.

The Supervisor's page makes a related point: the name on a tax bill is for mailing only. The true owner is whoever appears on the last recorded deed at the Recorder's office.

sections.h2: How is a Montgomery County home assessed?
sections.html:
Township assessors value the property, and the Supervisor of Assessments applies equalization factors so the level lands at 33 1/3 percent of market value. The assessed value minus any exemptions is the base for the levies. Each taxing body certifies what it needs, the Clerk turns those levies into rates within statutory limits, and the rate multiplied by the equalized assessed value gives the dollar tax on the bill.

A taxing district can raise its levy by up to 5 percent of what it received the year before. Anything above that triggers a Truth-in-Taxation hearing, which is informational and needs no vote. If your bill climbed, the county lists three usual causes: a higher rate from a referendum or levy increase, a higher assessment, or an exemption you are not receiving.

The county also notes how special areas work. A property in a TIF district pays the same total, but part of it goes to the TIF fund instead of the schools and county. Drainage district charges are set by the district and approved by the courts, and a property that is annexed to a district starts paying that district's rate.

sections.h2: How do you protest an assessment in Montgomery County?
sections.html:
Start with your township assessor, then go to the Supervisor of Assessments at (217) 532-9595, and file with the Board of Review if you still disagree. The Board of Review convenes on the first Monday of June and schedules further meetings as needed. By statute, a complaint for the current year must be filed within 30 calendar days of the publication of the assessment list (35 ILCS 200/16-55).

The Clerk's page describes a second route for the current year's tax: an objection filed at the Circuit Clerk, reachable at (217) 532-9546. A protest of future taxes goes to the Board of Review through the Supervisor's office. Because the paths differ, ask which one fits your situation before paying a fee.

Whichever way you go, the argument is about assessed value, not the size of the tax. The Supervisor suggests that neighbors who spot an under-assessed property tell the assessor, since errors in either direction shift the rate for everyone.

sections.h2: What happens when Montgomery County taxes go unpaid?
sections.html:
Unpaid taxes are offered at the annual tax sale held by the Treasurer. After a sale, the owner keeps the right to redeem for two to three years, depending on the property type, but at a higher cost because interest and fees pile on.

  • The Clerk issues an Estimate of Redemption for the parcel, and the page urges you to verify it is for the correct property.
  • Redemption is paid by cash, certified funds or money order made out to the Montgomery County Clerk, and there are no payment plans.
  • If the next year's second installment is also missed, the buyer can purchase that year at 12% interest.
  • Costs of any tax deed process are added to the redemption amount.

A notice called a Take Notice is mailed by the Clerk's office once taxes are sold, and the delinquent list is also published in local newspapers before the sale. Keep proof of every payment, because the county advises that a copy of the check or receipt is the best defense if a payment is not credited.

sections.h2: Which exemptions can a Montgomery County homeowner use?
sections.html:
The general homestead exemption applies to an owner-occupied principal residence, and in counties like this one the maximum reduction is $6,000 of equalized assessed value (35 ILCS 200/15-175). The Supervisor's office also helps applicants prepare the Senior Homestead Exemption and the Senior Citizens Assessment Freeze application.

The freeze application has to be filed every year, because household income can change when someone moves in or out. Ask the Supervisor's office which forms you need after a move.

sections.h2: What should a Montgomery County seller do about the tax bill?
sections.html:
Get the parcel number, pull the current and prior bills from the Treasurer, and ask the Clerk whether any year was sold. The title company then prorates the current year at closing, and the settlement statement shows what is paid or owed.

The deed also has to meet the Recorder's checklist. Any document with a legal description must carry the physical address and the parcel number, a completed Plat Act Affidavit is required on transfers, and a deed needs a "future taxes to" name and address. Margins matter too: two inches at the top of the first page and one inch after that. The property tax bill's description is not a complete legal description and will be rejected.

The Recorder offers a free Property Fraud Alert service that emails or texts you when a document is recorded under your name, which is worth setting up before and after a sale.

faqs.q: What is the phone number for the Montgomery County Treasurer?
faqs.a: The Treasurer's office answers at (217) 532-9521 and is in Room 101 of the Historic Courthouse in Hillsboro. For a copy of a current or past bill, the same office handles the request, and the automated payment line is (217) 627-6183.

faqs.q: Can Montgomery County taxes be redeemed with a payment plan?
faqs.a: No. The County Clerk says redemption must be made in cash, certified funds or a money order payable to the Clerk, and there are no payment plans for redemption. Ask for an Estimate of Redemption at (217) 532-9530 before sending money.

faqs.q: Who sets my Montgomery County tax rate?
faqs.a: The County Clerk calculates it. Each taxing body certifies a levy, and the Clerk's staff divides that by the assessed valuation, within statutory limits, then sends the result to the Treasurer, who prints and mails the bills.

faqs.q: Does a Montgomery County tax bill name the real owner?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. The Supervisor of Assessments says the name and address on the bill are for mailing only, and the owner of record is shown by the last deed at the Recorder's office.

faqs.q: Where do I file a complaint about my Montgomery County assessment?
faqs.a: File with the Board of Review through the Supervisor of Assessments at (217) 532-9595. Illinois law gives 30 calendar days from publication of the assessment list, and the Board convenes on the first Monday of June.
